feature.title: Six novels, published as "A Lady"
feature.lead: Austen's name never appeared on a book in her lifetime. Her first novel said only "By a Lady", and the next ones said "By the Author of" the earlier books. Each is free to read today.

items.label: Sense and Sensibility
items.text: Published by Thomas Egerton, "By A Lady". Austen paid the costs herself and the publisher took a commission on sales. All 750 copies sold by July 1813, and she made a profit of £140. It grew from an early draft in letters called Elinor and Marianne.

items.label: Pride and Prejudice
items.text: First written in 1796-97 as First Impressions, which a London bookseller turned down without reading. After long revision, Austen sold the copyright to Egerton for £110; she had asked for £150. The title page named it as by the author of Sense and Sensibility.

items.label: Mansfield Park
items.text: Her first novel written fully at Chawton, published by Egerton without her name. The first printing sold out within six months, and it earned her more than any of her other novels.

items.label: Emma
items.text: Published by John Murray, though the title page says 1816. Austen turned down Murray's offer of £450 for it and two older copyrights. She paid for 2,000 copies herself, kept the copyright and paid him a 10 per cent commission. After a hint from the Prince Regent's librarian, it was dedicated to the Prince Regent.

items.label: Northanger Abbey
items.text: Written as Susan around 1798 and sold to the bookseller Crosby for £10 in 1803. He never printed it, and the family bought it back for the same price in 1816. It was published after her death, together with Persuasion, by John Murray; the title page is dated 1818.

items.label: Persuasion
items.text: Begun on 8 August 1815 and finished on 6 August 1816, after she rewrote the ending. Her brother Henry chose the title after her death. His Biographical Notice in this edition was the first time her name was printed as the author of her novels.

items.label: Lady Susan (a seventh, shorter work)
items.text: A short early novel told in letters, written between about 1793 and 1795, about a clever and selfish widow. It was never published in her lifetime. Her nephew first printed it in the 1871 second edition of his Memoir.

timeline.title: Born at the rectory
timeline.text: Jane Austen was born at Steventon, where her father George Austen was the rector. She was the seventh of eight children, and her closest companion all her life was her older sister Cassandra.

timeline.title: A dangerous fever
timeline.text: Jane and Cassandra were sent to be taught by a Mrs Cawley in Oxford, who then moved to Southampton. Both girls caught typhus and were brought home. Jane nearly died.

timeline.title: A short time at school
timeline.text: The sisters went to the Reading Abbey Girls' School. They left before the end of 1786, because the fees were too high for the family. After that her education came from reading at home, guided by her father and brothers, with free use of her father's library.

timeline.title: The notebooks begin
timeline.text: From about 1787 to 1793 she wrote stories, plays and verse to amuse her family, later copied into three notebooks. The family also staged plays in the rectory barn. Her father gave the sisters good paper for writing and drawing.

timeline.title: Love and Freindship
timeline.text: At about 14 she wrote Love and Freindship, a short comic story in letters that mocks the fainting, over-emotional heroines of popular novels.

timeline.title: A comic History of England
timeline.text: She wrote The History of England, a parody of school history books, with small portraits painted by Cassandra.

timeline.title: Lady Susan
timeline.text: Between about 1793 and 1795 she wrote Lady Susan, a short novel in letters. It stayed in manuscript for the rest of her life.

timeline.title: Elinor and Marianne
timeline.text: She drafted a novel in letters called Elinor and Marianne, the seed of Sense and Sensibility. Sources disagree on the year: possibly 1795 or 1797.

timeline.title: First Impressions
timeline.text: She began First Impressions, the novel that would become Pride and Prejudice, and finished the draft in August 1797.

timeline.title: Refused unread
timeline.text: Her father offered First Impressions to the London bookseller Thomas Cadell. Cadell declined by return of post, without reading it.

timeline.title: Susan
timeline.text: She began Susan, a comic novel about a young reader of spooky novels. It later became Northanger Abbey.

timeline.title: Moving to Bath
timeline.text: In December 1800 her father announced that he would retire, and the family left Steventon for Bath. Austen found the move upsetting. Little is known of her Bath years, because Cassandra later destroyed Jane's letters from that time.

timeline.title: A proposal declined
timeline.text: She accepted a proposal of marriage from Harris Bigg-Wither, then withdrew her acceptance the next morning. She never married.

timeline.title: Sold for £10
timeline.text: Her brother Henry sold the manuscript of Susan to the publisher Benjamin Crosby for £10. Crosby advertised it but never printed it.

timeline.title: The Watsons
timeline.text: She began The Watsons, about a poor clergyman and his four unmarried daughters, and left it unfinished.

timeline.title: Her father dies
timeline.text: George Austen died. Jane, Cassandra and their mother now had little money of their own, and her brothers promised to support them.

timeline.title: Moving again
timeline.text: After stays in places such as Worthing, the women moved to Southampton, where they shared a house with her brother Frank and his new wife.

timeline.title: Asking for Susan back
timeline.text: She wrote to Crosby asking him to publish Susan or return it. He refused, and she could not afford to buy it back until 1816.

timeline.title: A home at Chawton
timeline.text: Her brother Edward gave his mother and sisters a cottage in the village of Chawton. With a settled home at last, Austen began to revise her old drafts and write new novels.

timeline.title: "By a Lady"
timeline.text: Sense and Sensibility was published by Thomas Egerton, credited only to "A Lady". Austen paid the costs and the publisher took a commission. It sold out, and she made about £140.

timeline.title: Pride and Prejudice
timeline.text: Her reworked First Impressions came out as Pride and Prejudice. She had sold the copyright for £110. The next day she wrote to Cassandra that she had "got my own darling child from London".

timeline.title: Mansfield Park
timeline.text: Mansfield Park was published. The first printing sold out within six months, and it became her most profitable novel.

timeline.title: Advice to a young writer
timeline.text: In letters to her niece Anna, who was writing a novel, Austen gave practical advice, including that a few families in a country village were the best subject to work on.

timeline.title: Persuasion begun
timeline.text: She started a new novel, which her family remembered her calling The Elliots. It became Persuasion.

timeline.title: An invitation from the Prince
timeline.text: The Prince Regent's librarian, James Stanier Clarke, invited her to visit the Prince's London home and hinted that she should dedicate her next book to him. She later mocked his many suggestions in a short satire, Plan of a Novel.

timeline.title: Emma
timeline.text: Emma was published by John Murray, dedicated to the Prince Regent. It was the last novel published in her lifetime.

timeline.title: A hard year
timeline.text: Her health began to fail. In March her brother Henry's bank failed, a blow to the family. That year the manuscript of Susan was finally bought back from Crosby.

timeline.title: Rewriting the ending
timeline.text: She finished a draft of Persuasion, then decided the ending was not right. She wrote two new chapters and finished on 6 August 1816. The cancelled chapters survive at the British Library, the only handwritten pages left of a novel she finished for publication.

timeline.title: Sanditon
timeline.text: She began a new novel about a seaside resort, later called Sanditon. On 18 March 1817 she put down her pen and did not return to it.

timeline.title: To Winchester
timeline.text: As her illness grew worse, Cassandra and Henry took her to Winchester for medical care. They stayed at a house in College Street.

timeline.title: Her death
timeline.text: Jane Austen died in Winchester, aged 41. The cause of her illness is not known for certain: later writers have suggested Addison's disease or Hodgkin's lymphoma, and sources disagree. She was buried in Winchester Cathedral.

timeline.title: Her name in print
timeline.text: Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published together. Henry's Biographical Notice of the author told readers, for the first time in print, that Jane Austen had written the novels.

timeline.title: A Memoir
timeline.text: Her nephew James Edward Austen-Leigh published A Memoir of Jane Austen. It brought her life to a wide public and led to new editions of her novels, which have never been out of print since 1833.

timeline.title: On the £10 note
timeline.text: Two hundred years after her death, the Bank of England put her portrait on its new £10 note, and a statue of her was unveiled in Basingstoke, near her birthplace.

works.title: The three notebooks (juvenilia)
works.text: Stories, plays and verse written in her teens to amuse her family, copied into three notebooks, Volume the First, Second and Third.

works.title: Love and Freindship
works.text: A comic story in letters, written at about 14, poking fun at swooning heroines and the fashion for strong feelings.

works.title: The History of England
works.text: A short parody of school history books, with portraits by Cassandra.

works.title: Lady Susan
works.text: A short novel in letters about a clever, selfish widow, first printed in 1871.

works.title: The Watsons
works.text: An unfinished novel about a poor clergyman's daughters, begun in Bath.

works.title: Sense and Sensibility
works.text: Two sisters, one sensible and one passionate, face love and money troubles. Her first published novel, "By a Lady".

works.title: Pride and Prejudice
works.text: Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy each learn to see past pride and quick judgment. Her best-known book.

works.title: Mansfield Park
works.text: Quiet Fanny Price, raised by rich relatives, holds to her own judgment. Her most profitable novel in her lifetime.

works.title: Emma
works.text: A confident young matchmaker gets nearly everything wrong and learns from it. Dedicated to the Prince Regent.

works.title: Plan of a Novel
works.text: A comic outline of the "perfect novel", built from the advice the Prince Regent's librarian kept giving her.

works.title: The cancelled chapters of Persuasion
works.text: Her first ending for Persuasion, replaced by two new chapters. The pages, dated July 1816, are held at the British Library (MS. Egerton 3038).

works.title: Northanger Abbey
works.text: A young reader of gothic novels learns the difference between stories and real life. Written as Susan in the 1790s, published after her death.

works.title: Persuasion
works.text: Anne Elliot meets again the naval officer she was persuaded to refuse eight years before. Published after her death.

works.title: Sanditon
works.text: An unfinished comic novel about a seaside resort, left off on 18 March 1817.

works.title: Letters
works.text: Her lively letters, mostly to Cassandra, about family, visits, books and her own novels. Cassandra is believed to have destroyed most of them; the rest were later collected by her great-nephew Lord Brabourne.
